Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১) Which structure is not related to formation of stomach bed?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The stomach bed refers to the structures lying posterior to the stomach, separated from it by the lesser sac (omental bursa). Classically, it includes the left dome of the diaphragm, spleen, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, pancreas (mainly the body and tail), splenic artery, transverse mesocolon, and the left colic flexure. The portal vein is not a component of the stomach bed. It lies posterior to the first part of the duodenum within the hepatoduodenal ligament and is not in direct relation to the posterior surface of the stomach.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Stomach bed includes:

    • Diaphragm

    • Spleen

    • Left kidney

    • Left suprarenal gland

    • Pancreas

    • Splenic artery

    • Transverse mesocolon

    • Left colic flexure

  • All are separated from the stomach by the lesser sac.

  • Portal vein is not part of the stomach bed.

Exam Pearl:
The portal vein is not a component of the stomach bed; the pancreas and splenic artery are classic posterior relations of the stomach.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ২) What is the arterial supply of the parts of gut developing from hindgut?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The hindgut is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). Embryologically, the hindgut extends from the distal one-third of the transverse colon to the upper part of the anal canal. Its derivatives include the descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. The IMA gives rise to the left colic, sigmoid, and superior rectal arteries, which supply these structures. In contrast, the coeliac trunk supplies the foregut, and the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) supplies the midgut. The inferior rectal artery is a branch of the internal pudendal artery and supplies the lower anal canal, not the entire hindgut.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Foregut → Coeliac trunk

  • Midgut → Superior mesenteric artery (SMA)

  • Hindgut → Inferior mesenteric artery (IMA)

  • IMA branches:

    • Left colic artery

    • Sigmoid arteries

    • Superior rectal artery

Exam Pearl:
Embryological arterial supply: Foregut = Coeliac trunk, Midgut = SMA, Hindgut = IMA.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ৩) Which is not a cardinal feature of large intestine?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The large intestine is characterized by three cardinal anatomical features: taeniae coli, haustra (sacculations), and appendices epiploicae (omental appendices). These features distinguish it from the small intestine. Plicae circulares (valves of Kerckring) are permanent circular folds of the small intestine, especially well developed in the jejunum, where they increase the surface area for absorption. They are absent in the normal large intestine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cardinal features of the large intestine:

    • Taeniae coli

    • Haustra (sacculations)

    • Appendices epiploicae

  • Plicae circulares → feature of the small intestine (jejunum > ileum)

  • Taeniae coli converge at the base of the appendix

Exam Pearl:
Plicae circulares are a hallmark of the small intestine, whereas taeniae coli, haustra, and appendices epiploicae are hallmarks of the large intestine.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ৪) What is the functional unit of liver?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport) is considered the functional unit of the liver because it best explains hepatic blood flow, oxygen supply, metabolic activity, and patterns of liver injury. It is a diamond-shaped unit supplied by terminal branches of the hepatic artery and portal vein, and is divided into Zones 1, 2, and 3. Zone 1 receives the most oxygenated blood, whereas Zone 3 is the least oxygenated and is most susceptible to ischemic injury and toxic damage. The classical hepatic lobule is the structural (anatomical) unit, while the portal lobule emphasizes bile secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Functional unit → Hepatic acinus

  • Structural (anatomical) unit → Classical hepatic lobule

  • Portal lobule → Functional unit for bile secretion

  • Acinar Zone 1 → First to receive oxygen and nutrients

  • Acinar Zone 3 → Most vulnerable to ischemia and drug toxicity

Exam Pearl:
For physiology and pathology, the liver's functional unit is the hepatic acinus; for anatomy, it is the classical hepatic lobule.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ৫) Which of the following is not a histological layer of gallbladder?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The gallbladder does not have a submucosa, making this an important histological distinction from most of the gastrointestinal tract. Its wall consists of mucosa, a fibromuscular layer (smooth muscle with connective tissue), perimuscular connective tissue, and an outer serosa on the free surface or adventitia where it is attached to the liver. The mucosa lies directly on the muscular layer without an intervening submucosa. This arrangement allows efficient concentration and absorption of bile.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gallbladder wall:

    • Mucosa

    • Fibromuscular (muscular) layer

    • Perimuscular connective tissue

    • Serosa (free surface) or Adventitia (hepatic surface)

  • No submucosa

  • No muscularis mucosae

  • Mucosa forms deep folds and may contain Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses

Exam Pearl:
The gallbladder lacks both a submucosa and a muscularis mucosae—this is a favorite anatomy/histology MCQ.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ৬) Major pancreatic duct opens into...... part of duodenum after combining CBD?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The major pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) usually joins the common bile duct (CBD) to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater). This ampulla opens into the major duodenal papilla located on the posteromedial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum. The flow of bile and pancreatic juice is regulated by the sphincter of Oddi. The accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini), when present, drains separately into the minor duodenal papilla, which is also located in the second part of the duodenum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Major pancreatic duct (Wirsung) + CBD → Ampulla of Vater

  • Opens into major duodenal papilla

  • Location → 2nd (descending) part of the duodenum

  • Controlled by sphincter of Oddi

  • Accessory pancreatic duct (Santorini) → Minor duodenal papilla

Exam Pearl:
The major pancreatic duct joins the CBD and opens into the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ৭) Which gut hormone causes Gall Bladder contraction & sphincter of oddi relaxation?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Cholecystokinin (CCK) is the gastrointestinal hormone responsible for gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, thereby facilitating the flow of bile and pancreatic enzymes into the duodenum. It is secreted by I cells of the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to the presence of fatty acids and amino acids in the intestinal lumen. In addition, CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and slows gastric emptying. Secretin mainly stimulates bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas, gastrin promotes gastric acid secretion, and somatostatin inhibits the release of several gastrointestinal hormones.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • CCK is secreted by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum.

  • Stimuli: Fatty acids and amino acids

  • Actions:

    • Gallbladder contraction

    • Sphincter of Oddi relaxation

    • Pancreatic enzyme secretion

    • Delays gastric emptying

  • Secretin → pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion

  • Gastrin → gastric acid secretion

  • Somatostatin → inhibits GI hormone release

Exam Pearl:
CCK is the key hormone that contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, promoting bile delivery into the duodenum.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ৮) All of the following digestive juices are alkaline except......?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Among the listed digestive secretions, saliva is the exception because it is usually neutral to slightly acidic (approximately pH 6.2–7.4), although it may become slightly alkaline with increased flow. In contrast, pancreatic juice (pH 7.8–8.4), succus entericus (intestinal juice) (pH about 7.5–8.0), and bile (pH about 7.6–8.6) are alkaline. The alkalinity of these secretions helps neutralize acidic gastric chyme entering the duodenum and provides the optimal pH for pancreatic and intestinal digestive enzymes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Saliva → Neutral to slightly acidic (may become slightly alkaline with high flow)

  • Pancreatic juice → Strongly alkaline due to bicarbonate

  • Bile → Alkaline; helps neutralize gastric acid and aids fat digestion

  • Succus entericus → Slightly alkaline

  • Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is stimulated mainly by secretin

Exam Pearl:
Pancreatic juice, bile, and intestinal juice are alkaline; saliva is the exception because it is generally neutral to slightly acidic.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ৯) Pendulum movement occurs in which part of the gut?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Pendulum movements are rhythmic to-and-fro contractions of the longitudinal muscle of the small intestine. Their primary function is to mix intestinal contents with digestive secretions and increase contact between chyme and the absorptive mucosal surface. Unlike peristalsis, pendulum movements produce little or no net forward propulsion. The small intestine also exhibits segmentation contractions, which are the major mixing movements. The stomach mainly exhibits peristaltic mixing waves, while the large intestine shows haustral contractions and mass movements rather than pendulum movements.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pendulum movement → Small intestine

  • Function → Mixing of chyme

  • Produced mainly by longitudinal muscle contraction

  • Segmentation → principal mixing movement of small intestine

  • Peristalsis → propulsive movement

Exam Pearl:
Pendulum movements are characteristic mixing movements of the small intestine and do not primarily propel intestinal contents.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১০) Insulin stimulated glucose uptake occurs by which transporter?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
GLUT 4 is the insulin-dependent glucose transporter responsible for insulin-stimulated glucose uptake. It is found primarily in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and adipose tissue. When insulin binds to its receptor, intracellular vesicles containing GLUT 4 translocate to the cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake. In contrast, GLUT 2 is insulin-independent and is present in the liver, pancreatic β-cells, kidney, and intestinal epithelium. GLUT 3 is the major neuronal glucose transporter with a high affinity for glucose, while GLUT 5 primarily transports fructose in the small intestine and sperm.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • GLUT 4 → Insulin-dependent; skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, adipose tissue

  • GLUT 2 → Liver, pancreatic β-cells, kidney, intestine; insulin-independent

  • GLUT 3 → Neurons; high-affinity glucose transporter

  • GLUT 5 → Fructose transporter; small intestine and sperm

  • Exercise also promotes GLUT 4 translocation independent of insulin

Exam Pearl:
GLUT 4 is the only major insulin-responsive glucose transporter and is found in muscle and adipose tissue.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১১) Basic factors that stimulate gastric secretion excludes.....?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The three major stimulatory regulators of gastric acid secretion are acetylcholine (ACh), gastrin, and histamine. Acetylcholine is released from vagal nerve endings and stimulates parietal cells via M3 receptors. Gastrin, secreted by G cells in the gastric antrum, stimulates parietal cells directly and indirectly by promoting histamine release from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells. Histamine acts on H₂ receptors of parietal cells, producing a potent increase in acid secretion. In contrast, secretin, released from S cells of the duodenum in response to acidic chyme, inhibits gastric acid secretion and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Three stimulants of gastric acid secretion:

    • Acetylcholine (M3 receptor)

    • Gastrin (CCK-B receptor)

    • Histamine (H₂ receptor)

  • Secretin → inhibits gastric acid secretion

  • Secretin also stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion

  • Histamine potentiates the actions of ACh and gastrin

Exam Pearl:
Remember the "gastric acid triad": Acetylcholine, Gastrin, and Histamine stimulate acid secretion; Secretin inhibits it.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১২) Which is the activator of trypsinogen?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Trypsinogen is an inactive zymogen secreted by the pancreas. It is initially activated by enterokinase (enteropeptidase), an enzyme present on the brush border of the duodenal mucosa. Enterokinase cleaves trypsinogen to form trypsin. Once a small amount of trypsin is formed, it autocatalytically activates additional trypsinogen and other pancreatic zymogens such as chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and procarboxypeptidase. HCl activates pepsinogen in the stomach, not trypsinogen, and carboxypeptidase itself is activated by trypsin.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Initial activator of trypsinogen → Enterokinase (enteropeptidase)

  • Site of enterokinase → Brush border of duodenum

  • Trypsin then activates:

    • Chymotrypsinogen

    • Proelastase

    • Procarboxypeptidase

    • Additional trypsinogen

  • HCl activates pepsinogen, not trypsinogen

Exam Pearl:
Enterokinase initiates trypsinogen activation; thereafter, trypsin activates itself and other pancreatic zymogens.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১৩) Typhoid ulcer is common in......?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Typhoid ulcers are classically found in the terminal ileum, which is part of the small intestine. After ingestion, Salmonella Typhi invades the Peyer's patches through M cells, proliferates within macrophages, and causes hyperplasia, necrosis, and ulceration of the lymphoid tissue. The ulcers are typically longitudinal (along the long axis of the bowel) and may lead to serious complications such as intestinal hemorrhage and perforation, particularly during the third week of illness. Although the colon may occasionally be involved, the terminal ileum is by far the most common site.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Common site of typhoid ulcer → Terminal ileum (small intestine)

  • Involves Peyer's patches

  • Ulcers are longitudinal

  • Major complications:

    • Intestinal hemorrhage

    • Perforation

  • Most severe during the 3rd week of untreated disease

Exam Pearl:
Typhoid fever characteristically produces longitudinal ulcers in the terminal ileum due to involvement of Peyer's patches.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১৪) Which is not one of the four features linked to H. pylori virulence?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Helicobacter pylori possesses several important virulence factors that enable it to colonize the gastric mucosa and cause disease. These include flagella, which provide motility through the gastric mucus; urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia, creating a locally alkaline environment that protects the organism from gastric acid; and adhesins, which facilitate attachment to gastric epithelial cells. Pepsin is not a virulence factor of H. pylori; it is a host-derived gastric proteolytic enzyme secreted by chief cells as pepsinogen and activated by hydrochloric acid.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Major H. pylori virulence factors:

    • Urease

    • Flagella

    • Adhesins

    • CagA

    • VacA

  • Urease → ammonia production → neutralizes gastric acid

  • Associated diseases:

    • Chronic gastritis

    • Peptic ulcer disease

    • Gastric adenocarcinoma

    • MALT lymphoma

Exam Pearl:
Pepsin is a host digestive enzyme, not an H. pylori virulence factor; remember the key virulence factors: urease, flagella, adhesins, CagA, and VacA.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১৫) Which is the most common site for gastric carcinoma?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The question is slightly ambiguous because the epidemiology of gastric carcinoma has changed over time. Traditionally, and in most MBBS/FCPS/BCS examination settings, the most common site of gastric adenocarcinoma is the antrum (distal stomach). This pattern is strongly associated with chronic Helicobacter pylori infection, chronic atrophic gastritis, and intestinal-type adenocarcinoma. However, in many Western countries, the incidence of proximal (cardia) gastric cancers has increased. For standard medical examinations, antrum remains the most accepted answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common site (traditional exam answer) → Antrum

  • Common histological type → Adenocarcinoma

  • Major risk factors:

    • H. pylori infection

    • Chronic atrophic gastritis

    • Smoking

    • Diet rich in smoked/salted foods

  • Diffuse type is associated with CDH1 (E-cadherin) mutation

Exam Pearl:
For MBBS, FCPS, MRCP, and BCS examinations, the most accepted answer is: Gastric carcinoma most commonly arises in the antrum.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১৬) Signet ring cells are found in.....?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Signet ring cells are the characteristic histological feature of diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma. These malignant cells contain abundant intracellular mucin, which displaces the nucleus to the cell periphery, giving the appearance of a signet ring. Diffuse gastric carcinoma infiltrates the stomach wall diffusely without forming a discrete mass, leading to linitis plastica ("leather bottle stomach"). In contrast, intestinal-type gastric carcinoma forms glandular structures and is associated with intestinal metaplasia and H. pylori infection. Although signet ring cells may rarely occur in other malignancies (e.g., colon, breast), their classical association is with diffuse gastric carcinoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Signet ring cells → Diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma

  • Intracytoplasmic mucin pushes nucleus to the periphery

  • Diffuse type → Linitis plastica (leather bottle stomach)

  • Associated with CDH1 (E-cadherin) mutation

  • Intestinal type → gland-forming tumor, often associated with H. pylori

Exam Pearl:
Signet ring cells are the hallmark of diffuse-type gastric carcinoma and are associated with linitis plastica.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১৭) Which is the most common site for carcinoid tumors?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
The question is slightly ambiguous because the answer depends on whether it refers to all gastrointestinal neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors or a specific anatomical subgroup. Based on current epidemiological data, the small intestine (especially the terminal ileum) is the most common site for gastrointestinal carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors. These tumors arise from enterochromaffin (Kulchitsky) cells and may secrete serotonin, producing carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, right-sided valvular heart disease) when hepatic metastases are present. The appendix is the most common site in many older anatomy/pathology MCQs and the most common site in children, but overall, small intestine is the most accepted answer in modern examinations.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common GI carcinoid site → Terminal ileum (small intestine)

  • Arises from enterochromaffin (neuroendocrine) cells

  • Secretes serotonin (5-HT)

  • Carcinoid syndrome usually occurs after liver metastasis

  • Diagnosis: Chromogranin A and 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA

Exam Pearl:
Modern exam answer: Small intestine (terminal ileum) is the most common site of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors; older MBBS questions may expect the appendix.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১৮) Which is not a feature of Crohn's disease?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Crohn’s disease is a chronic, transmural inflammatory bowel disease characterized by skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and prominent lymphoid aggregates. The characteristic ulcers are typically deep, linear or serpiginous, producing a cobblestone appearance of the mucosa. A broad-based ulcer is more characteristic of ulcerative colitis, where mucosal inflammation produces broad, shallow ulcers and pseudopolyps. Crohn’s disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly the terminal ileum and colon, and may produce strictures, fistulas, and non-caseating granulomas.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Crohn’s disease → Skip lesions

  • Inflammation → Transmural

  • Ulcers → Deep, linear/serpiginous

  • Mucosa → Cobblestone appearance

  • Marked lymphoid aggregates → characteristic

  • Ulcerative colitis → Broad, shallow ulcers and continuous involvement

Exam Pearl:
Crohn’s = transmural + skip lesions + deep linear ulcers; broad-based ulcers favor ulcerative colitis.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ১৯) Which is not alarming features in dyspepsia?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Jaundice is not considered a typical alarm feature of dyspepsia. Alarm features suggest a potentially serious underlying gastrointestinal disorder, particularly malignancy or complicated peptic ulcer disease. Important alarm features include unintentional weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia or gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent vomiting, progressive dysphagia/odynophagia, and a palpable mass. Jaundice may indicate hepatobiliary or pancreatic disease, but it is not a standard dyspepsia alarm feature. Therefore, among the given options, jaundice is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Dyspepsia alarm features:

    • Unintentional weight loss

    • Anemia/GI bleeding

    • Persistent vomiting

    • Progressive dysphagia

    • Palpable abdominal mass

  • Jaundice → suggests hepatobiliary/pancreatic pathology, not a classic dyspepsia alarm feature.

Exam Pearl:
In dyspepsia, weight loss, anemia, and persistent vomiting are alarm features; jaundice is not a classical alarm feature.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ২০) Which is not an indications for H. pylori eradication therapy?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.option4: Long-term NSAID or low-dose aspirin users
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
GERD alone is not an indication for H. pylori eradication therapy. Eradication is recommended when H. pylori infection is associated with peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori-positive dyspepsia, and in selected patients requiring long-term NSAID or low-dose aspirin therapy, particularly when ulcer risk is significant. H. pylori eradication may reduce ulcer risk in these settings. In contrast, H. pylori is not considered a primary cause of GERD, and eradication does not routinely improve GERD symptoms. Therefore, among the options, GERD is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • H. pylori eradication indicated in:

    • Peptic ulcer disease

    • H. pylori-positive dyspepsia

    • Selected long-term NSAID/aspirin users

    • Gastric MALT lymphoma

    • Previous gastric cancer in appropriate patients

  • GERD alone → not an indication

Exam Pearl:
Do not eradicate H. pylori simply to treat GERD; GERD is not a standard indication for eradication therapy.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ২১) Which is not a systemic complications of acute pancreatitis?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Hypercalcemia is not a typical systemic complication of acute pancreatitis. In severe acute pancreatitis, hypocalcemia is more characteristic and is associated with severe disease. It occurs partly because pancreatic fat necrosis releases fatty acids, which bind calcium and produce calcium soaps (saponification). Acute pancreatitis can cause systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), respiratory complications including hypoxia/ARDS, shock, renal failure, and metabolic disturbances. Hypoglycemia is not a classic hallmark but may occur in severe pancreatic dysfunction or critical illness. Among the given options, hypercalcemia is the clear exception.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Acute pancreatitis → Hypocalcemia

  • Mechanism → Fat necrosis → saponification

  • Severe disease → SIRS

  • Pulmonary complication → ARDS/hypoxia

  • Hypercalcemia → can be a cause of pancreatitis, rather than a typical complication

Exam Pearl:
Acute pancreatitis classically causes hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ২২) Which investigation is done to demonstrate anatomical abnormalities prior to surgical intervention in chronic pancreatitis?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography) is used to demonstrate the anatomical abnormalities of the pancreatic and biliary ducts before surgical intervention in chronic pancreatitis. It is non-invasive and provides excellent visualization of the main pancreatic duct, side branches, strictures, stones, and ductal dilatation. In contrast, ERCP is invasive and is now primarily used for therapeutic interventions such as stone extraction or stenting rather than routine diagnostic assessment. CT is excellent for assessing pancreatic calcification, atrophy, pseudocysts, and complications, but MRCP is particularly useful for delineating ductal anatomy before surgery.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • MRCP → Non-invasive assessment of pancreaticobiliary duct anatomy

  • ERCP → Mainly therapeutic now

  • CT → Excellent for calcification and complications

  • Chronic pancreatitis → ductal dilatation, strictures, stones, calcification

Exam Pearl:
For preoperative demonstration of pancreatic duct anatomy in chronic pancreatitis, MRCP is the preferred non-invasive investigation.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ২৩) Which is not a precipitating factor for hepatic encephalopathy?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Common precipitating factors for hepatic encephalopathy include dehydration, constipation, gastrointestinal bleeding, infection, electrolyte disturbances, renal dysfunction, and drugs such as sedatives. Constipation increases intestinal ammonia production and absorption, while dehydration can reduce hepatic and renal clearance of toxins. Drugs, particularly benzodiazepines, opioids, and other CNS depressants, can precipitate or worsen encephalopathy. Diabetes mellitus itself is not a recognized direct precipitating factor for hepatic encephalopathy, although diabetic patients may develop precipitating conditions such as infection, renal dysfunction, or electrolyte abnormalities.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Common precipitants:

    • Constipation

    • Infection

    • GI bleeding

    • Dehydration

    • Electrolyte disturbances

    • Sedative drugs

    • Renal dysfunction

  • Increased intestinal ammonia contributes to encephalopathy.

Exam Pearl:
Think of constipation, infection, dehydration, GI bleeding, and sedatives as classic precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy—not diabetes mellitus itself.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ২৪) Which hepatitis virus does not causes chronic infection?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Hepatitis A virus (HAV) does not cause chronic infection. It causes an acute, self-limited hepatitis, and patients generally develop lifelong immunity after recovery. In contrast, hepatitis B (HBV) and hepatitis C (HCV) can establish chronic infection. Hepatitis D (HDV) can also cause chronic infection when it occurs with chronic HBV infection. HAV is transmitted primarily by the fecal–oral route, whereas HBV, HCV, and HDV are mainly transmitted through blood and other body fluids.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • HAV → Acute infection only; no chronic carrier state

  • HBV → Acute or chronic infection

  • HCV → High risk of chronic infection

  • HDV → Requires HBV for replication; can become chronic

  • HAV → Fecal–oral transmission

Exam Pearl:
HAV never causes chronic hepatitis; HBV, HCV, and HDV can cause chronic infection.

Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.question: ২৫) Which test is non-invasive and most commonly used as a ‘first-line’ test to identify gallstones & biliary obstruction?
Alimentary, hepatobilliary & pancreas.exp:
Ultrasonography (USG) is the first-line, non-invasive investigation for suspected gallstones and biliary obstruction. It is highly effective for detecting gallbladder stones, gallbladder wall thickening, and biliary dilatation. It is inexpensive, widely available, does not involve radiation, and can be performed rapidly. CT is useful for complications and alternative diagnoses but is less sensitive for many gallstones. MRI/MRCP provides excellent visualization of the biliary tree and is useful when ductal stones or obstruction need further assessment. ERCP is invasive and is primarily used for therapeutic intervention, such as removal of common bile duct stones.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • USG → first-line for gallstones

  • Detects gallstones, gallbladder wall changes, and biliary dilatation

  • MRCP → non-invasive detailed ductal imaging

  • ERCP → mainly therapeutic

  • CT → useful for complications and alternative pathology

Exam Pearl:
Suspected gallstones → start with USG.
